{"found":true,"answer":"Your first version barely saved time because predicate pushdown was blocked in two places: staging de-duplication partitioned only by `order_id`, so date filtering could not skip old data, and the cutoff was a runtime scalar subquery rather than a compile-time literal. {"found":true,"answer":"The warehouse reaches the storage bucket through Snowflake’s storage integration, which assumes a read-only AWS IAM role using an external ID. No AWS keys or other long-lived credentials are stored in Snowflake. Terraform first creates the role with placeholder trust, then the integration generates the user and external ID, and Terraform tightens the role’s trust policy.","citations":[1,5]}

{"found":true,"answer":"Provisioning must happen in two passes because of a chicken-and-egg dependency. The Snowflake storage integration needs the IAM role’s ARN, but the role’s trust policy needs the Snowflake-generated user and external ID, which exist only after the integration is created. The first pass creates the role with placeholder trust; Snowflake then creates the integration and returns those values; the second pass tightens the role’s trust policy.","citations":[1]}

{"found":true,"answer":"Use a managed access schema. Create the schema with managed access enabled, make the deployment role its owner, and have that owner define future grants on new tables. A team might therefore expect only a few alerts monthly, or raise the threshold while accepting lower recall.","citations":[1,3]}

{"found":true,"answer":"Trust a “nothing unusual” result only if the test could have detected a real effect. If it misses effects such as 2× or 3× changes, a zero result proves little; the conclusion must be limited to effects the test had power to detect.
